title: Neurotoxicity of micro- and nanoplastics: evidence, mechanisms, and environmental relevance
content: Micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) have emerged as pervasive environmental contaminants that are now widely distributed across diverse ecosystems worldwide. Increasing evidence indicates that MNPs can enter biological systems through multiple exposure routes and accumulate in various organs, including the brain. To provide a comprehensive synthesis of current knowledge, we systematically searched the Web of Science Core Collection and PubMed for relevant literature published from database inception to 2026. The resulting evidence was reviewed to characterize the physicochemical properties, environmental distribution, and bioaccumulation of MNPs, with particular emphasis on their neurotoxic effects and underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms. Current findings suggest that MNPs can access the central nervous system by disrupting the blood–brain barrier (BBB) or via the olfactory nerve pathway. Once in neural tissues, MNPs may induce neurotoxicity through multiple mechanisms, including oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, disruption of protein signaling pathways, and modulation of the gut–brain axis. These processes may ultimately lead to behavioral abnormalities, neuronal damage, and an increased risk of neurodegenerative disorders. Despite the growing body of research, several critical challenges remain, including limitations in detection technologies, the diversity of MNP types, and the complexity of mixed environmental exposures. Future studies integrating multidisciplinary approaches will be essential to elucidate the neurotoxic mechanisms of MNPs more comprehensively and to inform evidence-based environmental and public health policies.
